text:
Regular conditional probabilities need not exist. Durrett credits the
first example to Dieudonn\'e (1948) and refers to Doob (1953), p.~624, and
Faden (1985) for later developments \cite[p.~214]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.
He locates the difficulty in the exceptional sets. For disjoint
\(A_1,A_2,\dots\in\mathcal S\), linearity and monotone convergence of
conditional expectation give
\(P(X\in\bigcup_nA_n\mid\mathcal G)=\sum_nP(X\in A_n\mid\mathcal G)\)
only almost surely, with a null exceptional set that depends on the
sequence. When \(\mathcal S\) contains uncountably many such sequences,
the union of their exceptional sets need not be null, so no single choice
of versions need be countably additive at almost every outcome
\cite[p.~214]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.
\Cref{thm:p15-w02c-p15-008-no-rcp} gives a probability space and a
sub-sigma-algebra for which no such kernel exists.

anchor_quote:
Thus a conditional law of the great-circle angle given its longitude
has the latter nonuniform density.
text:
Durrett calls this Example~4.1.8 \emph{Borel's paradox}
\cite[p.~210]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}. For a point uniform on the sphere
one might expect both the great-circle longitude and the angle along the
great circle to be uniform. The longitude is uniform but the angle is not.
Because the angle is independent of the longitude, its conditional law
given the longitude is its unconditional law, and that law puts more mass
near the equator than near the poles.\index{Borel's paradox}

text:
Durrett reads the conditioning sigma-algebra as the information at
one's disposal: for each event \(A\in\mathcal G\) one knows whether
\(A\) has occurred. A version of \(E(X\mid\mathcal G)\) is then the
\emph{best guess} of the value of \(X\) given that information
\cite[p.~207]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.
In the two requirements of the definition, \(\mathcal G\)-measurability
says that the guess uses only the available information, and the event
identity says that the guess is correct on average over every event the
information can distinguish (Durrett's conditions~(i) and~(ii)
\cite[pp.~205--206]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}).
For square-integrable \(X\) the reading has an exact form:
\cref{thm:p15-conditional-l2-projection} shows that the best guess is the
\(\mathcal G\)-measurable variable of least mean-square error, which is
Durrett's Theorem~4.1.15 \cite[p.~213]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.

Finally \(0\leq P(A\mid\mathcal G)\leq1\) almost everywhere for every event \(A\).

text:
The known-information and independence clauses are the two extremes
of Durrett's best-guess reading. When \(X\) is
\(\mathcal G\)-measurable the information determines \(X\), so the best
guess is \(X\) itself; a constant \(X=c\) is a special case
(his Example~4.1.3 \cite[p.~207]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}).
When \(X\) is independent of \(\mathcal G\) the information says
nothing about \(X\), and the best guess is the mean \(EX\)
(his Example~4.1.4 \cite[p.~208]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}).
Both are found by the method the source uses for conditional expectations
from Example~4.1.4 onward, which it calls \emph{guess and verify}: propose
a formula, then check that it is \(\mathcal G\)-measurable and that it
satisfies the event identity \cite[p.~208]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.
The annex proofs of linearity and of these two clauses take exactly that
form. The remaining clauses illustrate Durrett's remark, at the opening
of his Section~4.1.2, that conditional expectation has many of the
properties of ordinary expectation \cite[p.~210]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}:
linearity, preservation of order and the bounds
\(0\leq P(A\mid\mathcal G)\leq1\) mirror the corresponding facts
for \(E\).

text:
Durrett sums up the two identities as: the smaller sigma-algebra always
wins. He calls the first trivial. The second is easy to prove, and he
describes it, used together with his Theorem~4.1.14
(\cref{thm:p15-conditional-pullout}), as a powerful tool for computing
conditional expectations; he cautions that he has more than once seen it
invoked in proofs of false results \cite[p.~212]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.
One way to misapply it is to drop the nesting hypothesis: item~1 of
\cref{thm:p15-conditional-examples} gives two sigma-algebras for which
the order of conditioning changes the answer.
The identity \(E(C_{\mathcal G}X)=EX\) of
\cref{thm:p15-conditional-basic} is the second tower identity with the
smaller sigma-algebra \(\{\varnothing,\Omega\}\). Durrett notes that
conditional expectation has properties of this kind which have no
analogue for ordinary expectation \cite[p.~212]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.

text:
This is Durrett's Example~4.1.5, which relates the general definition to
the elementary one; he assumes every cell has positive probability
\cite[p.~208]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.
Its reading: the information in \(\mathcal G\) tells which cell contains
the outcome, and once the cell \(A_i\) is known, \(X\) is best guessed by
its average over that cell, namely
\(\int_{A_i}X\,dP/P(A_i)\) \cite[p.~208]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.
For \(X=\mathbf1_B\) that average is the elementary
\(P(B\cap A_i)/P(A_i)\), so \(P(B\mid\mathcal G)\) equals the
elementary conditional probability given \(A_i\) on each cell \(A_i\)
of positive probability.

Any other solution of the defining identity also serves. Put \(D_0=\{y:m(y)<\infty,\ a(y)<\infty\}\).

\(D_0\), and there the identity holds whatever the value \(k(y)\);
so \(k\) is arbitrary where \(m\) vanishes, and \(k=h\) on \(D\).
The function \(h\) above is one such \(k\).

text:
The first formula is Durrett's Example~4.1.6, and he motivates it by the
undergraduate rule \cite[p.~209]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}. Treat the density values as if
they were probabilities: the ratio \(f(x,y)/\int f(x,y)\,dx\) then plays
the part of the conditional probability that \(X=x\) given \(Y=y\), a
conditional density in \(x\), and integrating \(g\) against it suggests
\[
      E(g(X)\mid Y=y)=\int g(x)f(x,y)\,dx\Big/\int f(x,y)\,dx .
\]
The heuristic only proposes the formula; it is then verified against the
two defining requirements, as in the annex. Durrett states the example
under the simplifying assumption \(\int f(x,y)\,dx>0\) for all \(y\),
and his Remark after it drops that assumption in the form given by the
function \(k\) above \cite[p.~209]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.
The second formula is his Example~4.1.7 \cite[pp.~209--210]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.

Every event in \(\sigma(Y)\) is such a preimage, by the preceding
factorization proof's initial sigma-algebra identity.
This proves both defining conditions and hence the formula.
text:
\paragraph{Any solution of the defining identity.}
The set
\[
          D_0=\{y:m(y)<\infty,\ a(y)<\infty\}
\]
is Borel because \(m\) and \(a\) are measurable. If \(m(y)=0\), the nonnegative
section \(x\mapsto f(x,y)\) has integral zero, so it vanishes for
Lebesgue-almost every \(x\). Then \(|g(x)|f(x,y)=0\) for almost every
\(x\), so \(a(y)=0\), \(y\in D_0\), and
\(\int g(x)f(x,y)\,dx=0\). The identity
\(k(y)m(y)=\int g(x)f(x,y)\,dx\) at such \(y\) reads \(0=0\) for every
real \(k(y)\). This proves that \(k\) is unrestricted on
\(\{m=0\}\), and that \(h\) itself satisfies the identity on \(D_0\):
on \(D\) by its definition, and on \(D_0\setminus D=\{m=0\}\) because
both sides are zero.

Now let \(k\) be any real Borel function satisfying the identity on
\(D_0\). The set \(D\) is \(D_0\cap\{m>0\}\), and for \(y\in D\)
dividing by \(m(y)\in(0,\infty)\) gives \(k(y)=h(y)\). Hence
\(\{k(Y)\neq h(Y)\}\subseteq\{Y\notin D\}\), which has probability
zero by the first paragraph. The variable \(k(Y)\) is
\(\sigma(Y)\)-measurable as a Borel function of \(Y\). For every
\(A\in\sigma(Y)\), \(k(Y)\mathbf1_A=h(Y)\mathbf1_A\) almost everywhere,
so \(k(Y)\mathbf1_A\) is integrable and
\[
   \int_Ak(Y)\,dP=\int_Ah(Y)\,dP=\int_Ag(X)\,dP,
\]
the last equality being the defining identity already proved for
\(h(Y)\). Both defining conditions hold, so \(k(Y)\) is a version of
\(E(g(X)\mid Y)\).

text:
The total-variance identity is the special case of the nested identity
in which the smaller sigma-algebra is \(\{\varnothing,\Omega\}\);
Durrett presents it as an important special case of that identity
(his Exercises~4.1.6 and~4.1.7 \cite[p.~216]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}).
Apply the nested identity to the pair
\(\{\varnothing,\Omega\}\subseteq\mathcal G\). Conditioning on the
trivial sigma-algebra gives the constant \(EX\), and
\(E(C_{\mathcal G}X)=EX\), so the right side is
\(\operatorname{Var}(X)\) and the second term on the left is
\(\operatorname{Var}(C_{\mathcal G}X)\). Taking expectations in the
first display, with \(E(C_{\mathcal G}W)=EW\) for integrable \(W\), gives
\(E\operatorname{Var}(X\mid\mathcal G)=E(X-C_{\mathcal G}X)^2\),
which is the first term on the left.

text:
Durrett states the formula as his Exercise~4.1.8, where the sum is
called \(X\), and suggests understanding and remembering it through the
two special cases in which \(N\) or the summands are constant
\cite[p.~216]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.
If \(N=n\) is constant, then \(EN=n\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(N)=0\),
and the formula gives \(\operatorname{Var}(S)=n\sigma^2\), the variance
of a sum of \(n\) independent terms. If every \(Y_i\) equals the
constant \(\mu\), then \(\sigma^2=0\) and \(S=\mu N\), and the formula
gives \(\operatorname{Var}(S)=\mu^2\operatorname{Var}(N)\).
In general both sources of variation are present, and the two terms are
those of the total-variance identity of
\cref{thm:p15-conditional-variance} with \(\mathcal G=\sigma(N)\): the
annex proof finds \(\operatorname{Var}(S\mid N)=\sigma^2N\) and
\(E(S\mid N)=\mu N\), whose expectation and variance are
\(\sigma^2EN\) and \(\mu^2\operatorname{Var}(N)\).
